subject: keeping cattle as a household's savings and standing, not only as food
citation: Communal farmers' cattle-production perceptions, Ga-Matlala, Limpopo (PMC)
Livestock ownership determinants, OR Tambo District (Pastoralism, Springer)
Drought coping strategies and livestock resilience in SA (PMC)

farm_products: Growing of crops combined with farming of animals(mixed farming)

claims.text: Cattle are kept as a liquid asset for large expenses and inheritance, so any intervention that demands cash outlay is rejected unless it directly protects that income role.
objections: Does this require me to spend cash that I would otherwise keep in my cattle?

claims.text: Cattle theft is read as a symptom of youth unemployment and absent herders, so a solution is credible only if it absorbs idle youth labour or substitutes for the missing herder.
objections: Does this give the unemployed youth a reason to stop stealing my cattle?

claims.text: A household will own a livestock species only if its perceived utility—income, food, or cultural role—outweighs that of alternatives, so a new policy is judged by whether it lifts the utility of the species the household already prefers.
objections: Does this make the species I already keep more useful to my household?

claims.text: Resilience to drought depends on access to diverse resources, social networks, and finance, so a policy is seen as building resilience only if it widens those three channels; otherwise it is dismissed as inadequate.
objections: Does this give me access to finance or a network that I can lean on when drought hits?

confidence: Mixed-methods and survey-based, three study areas across Limpopo and Eastern Cape — mechanisms are consistent across contexts, but magnitudes and precise regional boundaries are not quantified.
